outcome: Nothing has settled whether 10 is solitary. Since 26 January 2024 four papers have narrowed what a friend of 10 (an m different from 10 with sigma(m)/m = 9/5) would have to look like, but none shows whether one exists; OEIS, last modified 12 October 2026, and Wikipedia, last edited 28 June 2026, still list 10 as unresolved and no friend of 10 is known.
problem_asks: Is 10 a solitary number? Unpacked: n is solitary when no positive integer m other than n has the same abundancy index sigma(m)/m = sigma(n)/n. For n = 10 the target value is sigma(10)/10 = 18/10 = 9/5. The single question is whether any m other than 10 satisfies sigma(m)/m = 9/5. If one exists, 10 is friendly; if none exists, 10 is solitary. The statement names no other quantity. The folklore answer is that 10 is solitary, but this is unproven.

events.what_happened: Jeffrey Ward, 'Does Ten Have a Friend?', arXiv:0806.1001. The abstract as opened states that any positive integer n other than 10 with abundancy index 9/5 must be a square with at least 6 distinct prime factors. Secondary sources (search snippets, not the full text) add that the smallest such prime is 5, that one prime factor is congruent to 1 mod 3, and that this prime appears with exponent congruent to 2 mod 6. Secondary sources describe the work as a 2007 REU project.
events.delivers: Necessary conditions on a hypothetical friend of 10: a square with at least six distinct prime factors (the smallest being 5, and the mod 3 detail from a search snippet only). It does not establish whether a friend exists.
events.remains: Whether any m other than 10 has sigma(m)/m = 9/5, which is the whole question. The restriction on shape does not decide existence.

checked_by.qualification: Authors of a later paper that sharpens Ward's bound from six to seven distinct prime factors
checked_by.what_they_did: Improved Ward's constraint on the number of distinct prime factors (as reported in their abstract and in search snippets)

events.direction: Narrows the shape of any friend of 10. It does not say whether a friend exists, so it does not cut either way on whether 10 is solitary.

events.what_happened: CemraJC, GitHub repository 'solidarity' (https://github.com/CemraJC/solidarity), a brute-force program in C++ and Python that searches for friends of a target number, with 10 as the default target. The README says the author checked for friends 'up to to 2,000,000,000' (quoted as written) and reports no outcome. The README calls the software 'very simple right now, and not very effective'. Wikipedia's Friendly number article cites a Cemra check dated 23 July 2022 in support of its statement about a 10^30 bound on the smallest friend of 10, though the article does not say which computation gives that bound.
events.delivers: A finite brute-force search over candidate friends up to about 2 x 10^9, if the README is accurate. It establishes no friend of 10 in that range and reports no result. It is a finite check of a universal question, so it does not decide whether 10 is solitary.
events.remains: Whether a friend of 10 exists beyond the searched range, which is the whole question.
events.directly_checkable: The program in CemraJC/solidarity can be rerun over the same range. I did not run it.
events.doubts: The README has no stated output and no visible commit dates. The 10^30 bound is attributed in Wikipedia to this check, while OEIS A074902 gives a 10^30 figure for other numbers up to 372 (see disputes). I could not confirm that this repository is the source of that figure.
events.direction: Rules out a friend of 10 only inside the searched range, and reports no finding. It cannot settle solitude.

events.what_happened: Tapas Chatterjee, Sagar Mandal and Sourav Mandal, arXiv:2404.00624. v1 (31 Mar 2024) is titled 'On the Friendly number of 10'. The current version v5 (17 Jan 2025) is titled 'A note on necessary conditions for a friend of 10'. The paper derives necessary conditions for a friend N of 10: N is an odd square with at least seven distinct prime factors, 5 being the least; if the exponent of 5 in N is 5^(2a) then a prime factor p of N satisfies a congruence with 5^f = 1 mod p; N has prime factors p = 1 mod 10 and q = 1 mod 6; if a Fermat prime F_k divides N then N has a prime factor congruent to 1 mod 2F_k; writing N = 5^(2a) m^2, m is not squarefree; Omega(N) >= 2 omega(N) + 6a - 4; and if Omega(m) <= K then N < 5 * 6^((2^(K-2a+1)-1)^2). The abstract says the paper does not prove that 10 is solitary and that no friend of 10 is known.
events.revisions: v2 6 Apr 2024; v3 13 Jan 2025; v4 14 Jan 2025; v5 17 Jan 2025 (retitled 'A note on necessary conditions for a friend of 10')
events.delivers: Necessary conditions on any hypothetical friend of 10: odd square, at least seven distinct prime factors (5 least), the congruence and Fermat-prime conditions, the Omega bound, and the size bound in terms of Omega(m). These narrow the shape of a friend, and they do not establish existence or non-existence.
events.remains: Whether a friend of 10 exists, which is the whole question.
events.doubts: No journal of record is identified for this preprint, and I found no independent public engagement. The v1 and v5 titles differ. I read only the v5 HTML and did not compare the versions.
events.direction: Narrows the shape of any friend of 10. It does not claim 10 is solitary and does not decide existence.

disputes.summary: Wikipedia's Friendly number article says that if 10 is not solitary its smallest friend is at least 10^30, citing a 2022 Cemra check. OEIS A074902 gives a 10^30 figure for other numbers up to 372, citing the same sequence, and says the sequence is not known to be complete up to 372. I found no paper and no repository output that states the bound for 10 directly, and the Cemra README reports no result. The two uses of the figure do not agree on scope.

summary: Searches for 'solitary number' first returned lonely-runner papers (Rosenfeld, Trakulthongchai; 8 to 13 runners). That is a different problem, so those papers are not events here, and I did not conflate them with this problem. The problem concerns abundancy: n is solitary if no m other than n has sigma(m)/m = sigma(n)/n, and for n = 10 the target is 9/5. Wikipedia lists 10 as the smallest number whose classification is unknown, conjectured solitary. The 2026 snapshots I opened (Wikipedia, last edited 28 June 2026; OEIS A074902, last modified 12 October 2026) still show it open, and the most recent post-window paper on 10 I found is the Oradea 2026 journal version of arXiv:2412.02701 (which states that the question is still open). Every post-window event on 10 is a restriction on a hypothetical friend, and none settles existence. Chatterjee, Mandal and Mandal (arXiv:2404.00624, posted 31 March 2024) give necessary conditions: an odd square with at least seven distinct prime factors, congruence conditions and a size bound. Mandal and Mandal (arXiv:2404.05771, 7 April 2024; Resonance 2025) bound the 2nd to 4th smallest prime divisors. Mandal (arXiv:2412.02701, 10 November 2024; Oradea 2026) bounds every prime divisor, and it is the only one of these with a public review, an AI referee (Pith Review, grok-4.3, 23 May 2026) that says no human had reviewed it yet. Mandal (arXiv:2504.08295, 11 April 2025) restricts the exponents mod 3. Two pre-window results bound the same object more strongly or first: Thackeray (arXiv:2310.15900, 24 October 2023; Indagationes Mathematicae 2024) shows at least ten distinct prime factors, and Ward (arXiv:0806.1001, 5 June 2008) gives the first constraint. A brute-force search by Cemra (README: up to 2,000,000,000, no reported result) is a finite check. Two papers on neighbouring numbers, 14 (arXiv:2503.11694) and 20 (arXiv:2409.04451), are recorded and discounted. Close calls: (a) Whether these restrictions move anything the problem names. The problem names one quantity, the existence of m with sigma(m)/m = 9/5, and none of these results touches it, so I record them as narrowing only. (b) Since the problem is about the set of friends, a lower bound on how many primes every friend must have is a step toward showing that set is empty, and a critic could read the Thackeray and Chatterjee results that way. I have not decided between these readings; the record gives both. (c) The 10^30 figure is attributed to different computations in Wikipedia and OEIS (see disputes), and I could not establish either source. AI: no source credits an AI system with any mathematics bearing on 10. I searched for AI involvement separately. OpenAI's 1 August 2026 list of ten solved problems (from news summaries, since the OpenAI page returned HTTP 403) contains no abundancy, friendly or solitary item. The 21 September 2026 claim of more than 100 resolved problems has no published list. The 6 October 2026 openai/math release (722 manuscripts, 372 families) has a catalogue (CONTENTS.md) that I read in full: family titles 001 to 377 contain none of abundancy, perfect, friendly or solitary numbers, though I checked family titles only, not every constituent manuscript title. AlphaProof Nexus (arXiv:2605.22763, 21 May 2026, v2 8 June 2026) proves 44 of 492 OEIS conjectures, but the abstract names no sequence and its PDF body and GitHub mapping file (404) were unreadable, so whether any of those 44 concerns friends or solitary numbers is unresolved. The only AI engagement found with any paper on 10 is the Pith AI review of arXiv:2412.02701, which is checking and not mathematics in the result; the AI-generated Moonlight review of the 14 paper is likewise a summary, not a contribution. For each of the human papers I opened the HTML or abstract, and none names an AI system in its acknowledgements or methods. The Thackeray PDF was unreadable, so its acknowledgements are unverified. None of the events credits a system with a result, so ai.systems is empty throughout.
competing_reading: The strongest case for treating the Chatterjee-Mandal-Mandal, Mandal-Mandal, Mandal (2412.02701 and 2504.08295) and Thackeray results as real progress on the problem: the question is about the existence of friends, and each of these results removes possible friends, so as a set of constraints they cut toward 10 being solitary. On that reading the sequence 2008 (Ward) to 2025 is a steady narrowing of a set that may be empty, with the prime-factor count rising from 6 to 10. The strongest case against: none of these results touches the named quantity, which is whether any m with sigma(m)/m = 9/5 exists, and each one says in its own abstract that existence is open. Restricting a hypothetical object is not the same as showing the object is absent. Note also that the Pith review says the 2412.02701 results rest on imported lemmas, and that the 10-prime-factor result is cited secondhand in the search results.
what_would_settle_it: A proof that no m other than 10 has sigma(m)/m = 9/5 would make 10 solitary; an explicit m with that abundancy would make it friendly. Short of that, the evidence that would move the status is (i) the full text of Thackeray's Indagationes Mathematicae paper, to check the 10-prime-factor argument and its acknowledgements; (ii) the AlphaProof Nexus OEIS list (44 proved conjectures), to see whether any concerns sigma or friendly numbers; (iii) the per-manuscript titles of the openai/math catalogue; and (iv) an explanation of the 10^30 figure, namely whether it comes from a published or reproducible computation for 10 specifically.
